Alan Grey Ph.D.

Alan Grey  

Ari Kiev: Transcultural Psychiatry New York: The Free Press, 1972. 223 pages, $7.95 (cloth), $2.95 (paper).

IS IT POSSIBLE FOR A scientific treatise to be anchored to unscientific premises and still offer some useful and interesting information to the reader? Well, "Transcultural Psychiatry" is a fine example of the genre. When a work intends to be scientific, it is a serious charge to suggest that it is not. Therefore, in fiarness to Dr. Kiev, let him state his position in his own words before it is questioned. Here's this puzzling bit of reasoning on the first page of his text:

Firm etiological knowledge, of the sort that would permit more certain classification and diagnosis, is still a hope for the future. It is therefore essential to define certain basic assumptions about psychiatric disorders that will serve to delimit the kinds of inferences that can be drawn from the material considered in this book, and at the same time to emphasize the distinction that needs to be made between sociocultural and psychological phenomena.

The italics are my own, to mark off sources of confusion. After a reassuringly sophisticated reference to etiological ignorance, the writer might be expected to recommend an open-minded, multidimensional investigation of psychiatric disorders, at least until the evidence warrants a more selective focus. Particularly so, since cross-cultural psychiatry is an interdisciplinary enterprise, lending itself well to such broad-gauge study. Instead, the second sentence urges that this condition of ignorance requires not a series of questions but a set of assumptions!

And yet uneasiness would seem premature so early in the book.

David Liberman  

IN THIS PAPER I WILL support the notions: (a) that some features of the verbalizations in analysis allow us to understand unconscious phantasies; (b) that these traits are valuable when we research psychoanalytic dialogue so as to transmit empirical data in scientific communications, and (c) that what I suggest in (a) has further consequences for effecting strategic, technical, and tactical approaches with which to break up Id resistances (compulsion to repeat).

Introduction

a. The paralinguistic elements1 of adult verbalization have an earlier root than articulate language; they somehow resemble infantile ways of communicating inasmuch as they constitute a manner of codifying experiences that cannot as yet be put in verbal language. They provide support for the objectivization of the qualities of unconscious phantasies. One of the advantages of this approach lies in the fact that we can effect deductive inferences on empirical bases in the dialogue during the course of the analytic treatment. I shall, as I have written elsewhere (Liberman, 1962), (1966), (1971), introduce here some findings from different currents of contemporary linguistics which I consider to be useful

All rights of reproduction in any formed reserved.

1By paralinguistic elements of the patient's verbalization I mean the universe of phenomena which were described by Pittenger, Hockett, and Danehy (1960). The elements which I have found most useful are considerations about strength, loudness, rhythm, pitch, length of sounds, length of silences, sighs, whispering, and tremolos. We can also take into account openness, breathiness, articulation, interruptions in the passage of air, and nasalization, as well as the range of deviations from the average for the patient concerned.2The term "unconscious phantasy" is used here following Isaac (1952). She said, "Phantasies are not dependent upon words, although they may under certain conditions be capable of expression in words. The earliest phantasies are experienced in sensations: later, they take the form of plastic images and dramatic representations. Unconscious phantasies exert a continuous influence throughout life, both in normal and neurotic people, the differences lying in the specific character of the dominant phantasies, the desire or anxiety associated with them and their interplay with each other and with external reality." See also "On the Ontogenesis of Fantasy, " Benassy and Diatkine, which has several points in common with my own view. "If fantasy has a history, if unconscious fantasy is timeless, and if language introduces serial order, we see why fantasies should be analyzed one at a time, at what Heimann calls the 'patient's actual point of growth'. It could be suggested that the emotional content, expressed through language and body behaviour, as well as the whole context sometimes enables the analyst to date the phantasy, and that a very ordinary and ungrammatical language, referred in the end to the patient's and the analyst's body images in a free relationship, enables the patient to introduce his own timing into his own analyst's, to 'assume an active role in his cure'." (Symposium on Fantasy, 23rd International Psycho-Analytical Congress, Stockholm, July—August 1963.)

The Unconscious in History11

Lancelot Whyte

Lancelot Whyte

Lancelot Law Whyte
93, Redington Road
London, N.W.3
England

Lancelot Whyte  

SOCIOLOGY WOULD BENEFIT from a more comprehensive theory of cumulative social change in the course of history. We are here concerned with social and historical changes over decades and centuries, not with the much longer term evolutionary changes due to modifications in the human genetic inheritance. The question is: What makes history the story of change? The main factors are technological changes and the growth of knowledge. But these are the consequences of a deeper primary cause: the human imagination and its ability to form novelties and to accumulate them. This covers a great range of achievements, unconscious and conscious, from the early development of language and tools to all new inventions, words, ideas, and methods. This ability arises from the formative mental processes of individuals—here called the imagination.

We may ask: Is this accumulation always conscious, or is there also an unconscious accumulation? Can the products of the imagination be accumulated without awareness? To clarify this some distinctions must be drawn.

1. It has been well established during this century that pathological mental processes, the sources of which lie in unconscious processes, play an important role in the individual life. Freud's work lay mainly in this realm, where unconscious conflicts distort behavior. I am using the term "pathological, " which is a matter of degree, to refer to particular mental processes and components of behavior which reveal dissociation, conflict, and distortion.

Yale Kramer  

I WAS TROUBLED BY the title of this symposium. It seemed to imply that one can easily distinguish what is rational from what is irrational in psychoanalytic education. The fact is that there is very little that is "rational" in life, or in psychoanalytic education, if by rational we mean demonstrably proved beyond a reasonable doubt, by the systematic accumulation of evidence. And that which is rational, using such a definition, is probably not worth discussing. Those issues which still excite our interest and debate—those which are under discussion today—are probably the ones which are very un-rational and ambiguous.

I am sure we have all had the opportunity of treating patients who use reason and rationality in a defensive way, and from such experiences we know how often rationality can be used in the service of, or can mask, profound irrationality. Often such terms as rationality and irrationality contain subtle explicit or implicit value judgments. I suggest that we beware of the possibility that lurking behind our use of "rational" and "irrational" as these terms apply to psychoanalytic education, are professional value judgments of either a theoretical or practical nature; that what we might really mean by "rational" is "what I like."

It is probable that what passes for psychoanalytic education is a set of operations having various admixtures of the rational and irrational. Lacking any harder information at this time I suspect it would be very difficult to distinguish one from the other.

TO STUDY WHAT HINDERS the growth of candidates we need to consider separately the intrapsychic problems of candidates and the external situation of institute training. It is essential not to use the external problems of the institute so as to avoid confronting candidate's intrapsychic conflicts. It is equally essential not to use

260

candidate's intrapsychic problems so as to avoid facing what is wrong with the psychoanalytic institute training situation.

Dr. Lefer suggests that, hopefully, the candidate brings to psychoanalytic training a "willingness to learn" and that the task of supervision is to promote self-inquiry.

But that is what so much of the problem is about—that most candidates initially have problems with their willingness to learn. Psychoanalytic candidates become students in their thirties, having already been students most of their lives, at a time when they are already qualified professionals, often responsibly involved in the teaching of psychotherapy. Psychoanalytic training requires considerable time, money, effort, and energy. Many start analytic training after military service, where there are extensive clinical responsibilities and one is looked to as expert in the practice of psychiatry. Many have been administrators in hospitals, clinics, and mental health centers, as well as teachers in medical schools. Analytic training is initiated at a time when one has finally been able to earn money; when professional status and power are, to one's delight, increasing. One comes to analytic training with unrealistic expectations of analysis and of the process of becoming an analyst. Unlike professional colleagues in other fields, the candidate's major task is a painful one confronting those aspects of himself he has needed most to keep hidden. The first lesson for the analytic candidate to learn is how much he does not want to learn, and how much he will have to struggle against this tendency for the rest of his life. He will also have to learn how irrational is much of his motivation for becoming an analyst. There is much to relinquish at the beginning of analytic training. The candidate may then fantasy that after four or five years of training, when he graduates, he will regain what he has given up of his neurotic hopes.

Marianne Eckardt M.D.

Marianne Eckardt

Marianne Horney Eckardt, M.D.
200 East End Avenue
New York City, N. Y. 10028

Marianne Eckardt  

YOU, WHO ARE GRADUATING TODAY, cherish the belief that you have learned some of the fundamentals of psychoanalysis as a start toward becoming wise therapists. I believe this to be true. You have received as good a training as can be given at this time.

Now, I know that we all want to feel reasonably certain that our knowledge is accurate and relevant. This assurance, however, I cannot give you. You are graduating at a time of world change, at a time when the value of psychoanalysis is being questioned, and at a time when psychoanalysis is reexamining its own knowledge. This reevaluation does not ask, "Are we right or wrong?" It looks at the nature of the knowledge which has been transmitted. Certainty will not be in your grasp, but the coming period promises to be one of active creative debate, creative thinking, observation, dialogue, and clinical ingenuity in which you will be a participant. You have not learned a trade; you have learned to sharpen your minds, to observe, to listen, to question, to evaluate, to see relationships, and to work in full partnership with another human being so that he may shape his life more to his liking.

You have already begun to develop a style of your own, but you are still too close to your institution not to have adopted its lingo and its favorite formulations. A few words about the use of lingo. If you can, avoid it. It has more pitfalls than benefits. Supposedly, it exists to provide a common frame of reference, to facilitate communication. But psychoanalytic terms have a historical life of their own and mean different things to different people.

I AM DELIGHTED that Dr. Braun has emphasized the practical therapeutic lessons to be drawn from Strindberg's descriptions of his mental crisis and the processes by which he recovered from it.

One fundamental lesson to be learned, and relearned, is that the boundary between madness and sanity is often not sharp and absolute, nor final. The mad person is by no means a total stranger. Strindberg spoke to this point in his remarkable essay, "Psychic Murder: (Apropos 'Rosmersholm')." Commenting on the effects of isolation he said,

Soon come false causal associations, erroneous conceptions, conclusions without sufficient basis, delusions of sight and hearing, and finally madness or a constant mania for defending oneself that finds expression in attacking other people.

Then he added,

All of these symptoms occur sporadically and to mild degrees in all people, for even if upbringing has made the human being human, upbringing is only an encumbrance which can fall off like a loose garment in moments of strong passion (Strindberg, 1968).

After World War I he entered Trinity College, Cambridge, where he studied under Rutherford, and later entered Göttingen, Germany.

Imprisoning Abstractions

Raymond Moore Ph.D.

Raymond Moore

Raymond Moore, Ph.D.
320 Equitable Building
Des Moines, Iowa 50309

Raymond Moore  

HUMAN BEINGS ARE capable of developing some very distorted ideas about living. We spoil many opportunities because we approach them with emotionally charged stereotypes and biases. As therapists we try to help patients rethink and reevaluate self defeating fixations and transferences so they can "bring their thinking up to date, " as Fromm-Reichman (1950) put it so long ago. I hope that the following discussion of concept boundary formation and ego boundary formation will be of some use to therapists in their work with patients so that they can dispell those limiting beliefs which imprison them.

One important distinction has become obscured in our language. Heidegger (1968) has pointed out that the word "being" can be used as either noun or verb, as can a large number of words. Nouns should not be used in reference to people or their being. Verbs are acceptable because they speak of action, behavior, and functioning, but nouns sound as if being could be frozen into a make-believe abstract substance. Yet the noun is so ingrained in our language habits and thought that we blindly accept this error. Take the noun "mind." A mind is not a substance. It is actually a "verb" composed purely of functions, such as perception, memory, ego defenses, fantasy, etc. This error of treating people as objects, or nouns, comes from the mind's function of forming abstract concepts and retaining these in memory. Because the mind is capable of this function of retaining abstract concepts, a person is able to be in the world as though he were some sort of substance. Through abstract conceptualization, and retention of these abstractions in memory, we can actually imitate a substance or object. To the Editors:

Dr. Witenberg's address at the William Alanson White Institute graduation of 1971, entitled "Horoscopes and Other Scientific Phenomena" (Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Vol. 8, No. 2) seems to warrant a reply from someone at the other end of the scale; someone to whom the speech was addressed, like myself.

As a recent graduate I have reflected on his message and wondered how much do I feel as he does and where along the road did we part company? At best, I suppose I can put my finger only on his description of himself as a "manager"—"someone who thinks he knows right from wrong"—and someone who is predicting the future to "motivate through hope or fear those who would be apathetic."

Reading this, I am reminded of Emile Durkheim's statement: "God is society worshipping itself." Can one assume that without "management" people would become apathetic or even hopeless?

I write this with a full appreciation of the unique climate Dr. Witenberg has created at the White Institute, a climate which enables budding analysts to grow and to flower into full bloom. Nathan G. Hale, Jr.: Freud and the Americans London: Oxford University Press, 1971.

Max Schur: Freud: Living and Dying New York: International Universities Press, 1972.

IN 1909 FREUD MADE HIS ONLY visit to America, to deliver the Clark lectures. In 1916 he delivered a revised version of them at the University of Vienna. The American lectures introduced psychoanalysis to American psychiatrists, psychologists, social scientists, and neurologists. They were extensively covered by the press, and led to the creation of a movement, and to the doctrine's popularization. The Viennese lectures, at first attended by many, had few listeners at the end. One of the latter was the medical student Max Schur, who later on as Freud's physician and still later as a trained analyst, was in the unique position to enrich our biographical knowledge of Freud.

While Schur's psycho-biography adds primarily to our knowledge and to the legend of Freud as a person, Hale's Freud and the Americans is primarily cultural—historical. Both books increase our understanding of Freud and Freudiana, and will themselves lead to new polemics and reinterpretations of psychoanalytic history and theory. To the extent that Freud's theory of the unconscious has been diffused in myriad ways and has been held responsible for societal ills, sexual liberation, repressive sublimation, racism, and sexism, to that extent reexamination of the original sources within their cultural contexts are necessary. As both history and legend grow, the difficulty of separating the two increases.

INCREASINGLY SINCE THE 1950's the impact of the patient on the analyst has been considered an area of valid study. With the reciprocal nature of relationships being generally accepted by analysts

369

of all persuasions, with operationalism in full bloom, it became convincing that patients have impact on analysts in the same way that analysts have impact on patients. The discussions continue. The problem remains. How much of this impact does the analyst reveal, and how does he do it.

While Sullivan himself admonished us against sharing, e.g., feelings of anger, some of his formulations stand us in good stead. His concept of participant—observer is very useful in this respect. At any given moment in psychoanalysis there is a mix of these two aspects of our behavior. How much of each is determined by the goal of the treatment, that is, the uniquely analytic goal—the making available of hitherto inattended and dissociated aspects of the personality. Prior to the achievement of this goal, many factors come into play as a result of the process. They are the result of an explicit sharing of the reason for the mutual effort, the detailed anamnesis, the coming into touch with the core of the patient, the establishment of a cooperative relationship, the changes evoked in the analyst by the patient, and the change in behavior by the patient which is followed by the cognitive integration of the inattended and the dissociated—called insight. Throughout all this process the analyst is influenced by the power of the unconscious processes and attitudes of the patient. Does he reveal this impact? Freud, Sullivan and others stood for reserve, tact, empathy, interest, curiosity but not sympathy, conversation, or mere exchanges of sentiment and anxiety. Considerations as to whether the interventions were for the narcissistic gain of the analyst were weighed. How many distortions from the past were in the analyst's head and how many did he display with a caveat against the display. Then a moderate loosening of the injunction arose: "Use the feelings invoked in you to point out what the patient is doing." Our culture changed. Encounter groups, peer groups developed; even our social manners changed. With these changes came expectations of "instant intimacy, " "complete candor" and devil take the hindmost. Reserve and tact lost their value. And this has had its impact on analysis.

Charles C. Dahlberg: From Food to Fertilizer—The Role of Excrement in the Life Cycle.

Reading, Mass.: Young Scott Books, 1973. 72 pages.

AS ITS TITLE IMPLIES, the major purpose of this little book is to describe the important role of excrement in the life cycle. This subject has not been given the attention it deserves because of inappropriate inhibitions, and perhaps Dr. Dahlberg has started a trend long overdue.

The author begins with a basic description of the life cycle, highlighting the vital role of excrement. He then describes: the human digestive system, with special focus on the way in which excrement is produced; the role of bacteria, with emphasis on their relationship to waste products; sewage disposal systems; animal excreta; and the uses for manure. The book concludes with a chapter discussing our attitudes toward excrement, in which Dr. Dahlberg attempts to explain the psychological reasons for our embarrassment over our body wastes.

As I read this book I kept wondering about the age group for which it was written. The format, large print, and illustrations by Albert F. Michini strongly suggest that this is a children's book. Parenthetically instructing the reader on the correct pronunciation of such words as feces, urine, and anus also suggests that the book is written for youngsters, as does the frequent use of words like belly, squishing, and mushy. However, Dr. Dahlberg discusses quite complicated biochemical mechanisms and even though he attempts to reduce these to the most simplified terms, I cannot imagine most prepubertal children even beginning to grasp their import.

THIS IS AN INTRODUCTION to the four papers that follow, by Drs. Bleger, Grinberg, Liberman, and Zac, members of the Argentine Psychoanalytic Association, which represent—despite the diversity of their themes—specific modes of conceptualization characteristic of a collective point of view known as the "Argentine School of Psychoanalysis." The four authors address themselves to different issues: Bleger elaborates a theoretical approach to the area of psychosis; Grinberg deals with the problem of identity; Liberman is concerned with linguistic parameters, as a way of establishing a more clearly scientific basis for the psychoanalytic method; Zac addresses problems in the development of thinking. These authors demonstrate clearly the application of multidisciplinary thinking to the growth of psychoanalytic ideas. Their adoption of the multidisciplinary perspective in no way compromises their adherence to object relations theory as the foundation of the psychoanalytic movement in Argentina.

In the course of institutionalization of psychoanalysis by means of the organization of the International Psychoanalytic Association, conceived and promoted by Ernest Jones, the power structure of the psychoanalytic movement tended, from the outset, to become verticalized. This principle of organization, precipitated and perpetuated the problem of conflicting factions within the British Psychoanalytic Association. One pole of the conflict—the majority group—was represented by Anna Freud, whose followers in England had strong ties with the dominant psychoanalytic force in the United States, embodied in the American Psychoanalytic Association.

Martin Grotjahn M.D.

Martin Grotjahn

Martin Grotjahn, M.D.
416 N. Bedford Drive
Beverly Hills, Calif. 90210

Martin Grotjahn  

SINCE THE SECOND WORLD WAR, several kinds of sexual behavior are no longer considered pathological but are now accepted within the frame of normality. This is not simply because our attitudes have changed. It constitutes, in my opinion, an actual change in pathology. There are signs that a new pathology is developing.

CLINICAL OBSERVATIONS

When I listened to my patients before World War II and learned via their anamnesis that they had daily (or nightly) sexual intercourse, I invariably took it to indicate "hypersexuality." I did not consider it a symptom which demanded therapeutic intervention, but I did indeed take it as a clue that I probably would eventually find considerable sexual pathology and anxiety on further investigation. At that time high sexual frequency would suggest that such a person was fighting off feelings of sexual inferiority, doubts about sexual competence, or feelings of general alienation and unrelatedness. Often deeply disturbing homosexual trends could be found which the patient could neither accept nor repress. He had to deny these trends to himself and to his wife by daily sexual activity. If I continued to investigate, my assumption in such situations almost unfailingly was demonstrated as correct. My evaluation and reconstruction of the dynamics would have been accepted by most of my colleagues. Quite generally, satyriasis or nymphomania were considered to be defenses against latent homosexuality. I am not suggesting that these dynamics were incorrect. It is my contention that these dynamics are no longer valid.

A reassurance emerges today from our connection with the animal world. I am thinking not only of the provision in such books of an ancient lineage for the sacredness of tribal and personal property. THERAPY, broadly defined as the remedial treatment of bodily disorders, can be specifically classified in many ways, depending upon one's prejudices, preconceptions, and increasing understanding of the disease process. Thus we can determine etiological therapy when we have definitively established the cause of a disorder, in contrast to symptomatic therapy, which is designed to alleviate specific discomforts associated with the disorder. This is precisely the situation when isoniazid is used to kill the tubercule bacillus, while codeine is administered to relieve the distressing and disabling cough that accompanies tuberculosis.

Such a significant distinction may be distorted and perverted when etiology is unknown, disputed, or still in the process of being established. This is the case in psychiatry with all but a minute fraction of the organic disorders of the brain. Who today would have the consummate arrogance to assign a specific cause to schizophrenia? Who would presume to claim flatly that schizophrenia is one disease and not a cluster of related disorders?

When we come to that treatment modality called psychotherapy, who is to say what procedure or technique is fully etiological or symptomatic. Webster defines psychotherapy "as a treatment designed or serving to bring about social adjustment." With this definition, we can begin to understand the complexities involved in classifying the variety of therapies, since it not only involves the definition of the causes of a disorder, but also the goals of treatment. THE PURPOSE OF THIS PAPER is to elaborate ideas presented in an earlier article (Counts, 1973) published in this Journal. I am prompted to do so to express more clearly what may have been poorly elucidated in the original essay, and to respond to the discussants (Zaphiropoulos 1973), (Siegel, and Harrell, 1973).

In the original paper I suggested that family therapy was more useful with families made up of individuals who were poorly individuated and who extensively used defenses such as projection and externalization, so that they tended to see the sources of their difficulties as arising externally to themselves. I suggested that family therapy was effective as a means of preparing patients for individual treatment who were otherwise resistant to individual psychotherapy.

While I am in agreement with many points made by Dr. Zaphiropoulos in his discussion, I would like to respond to some of his observations.

He states, "In conjunction with this concern, I wish to mention briefly the importance of the concept of boundaries as containing and constricting borders."

I would put the issue somewhat differently. I do not consider rigid, inflexible ego boundaries as demonstrating a well-developed sense of individuation. Quite the contrary.

Henri F. Ellenberger: The Discovery of the Unconscious: The History and the Evolution of Dynamic Psychiatry. New York: Basic Books, 1970. 932 pages, $15.00

THIS BOOK, a historical treatment of the unconscious, is oriented, as the subtitle indicates, to a psychiatry which is dynamic and preoccupied with psychic energy, rather than a psychiatry chiefly concerned with the organic and static. Motivated by the fact that the evolution of dynamic psychiatry has undergone more metamorphoses than any other science and that the history of dynamic psychiatry is unparalleled among sciences for its errors, gaps, and legends, Professor Ellenberger undertook the project of writing a complete survey of dynamic psychiatry. As such, we have been presented with, first of all, a monumental history of dynamic psychiatry. Secondly, the work reconstructs and explicates in detail its four great systems, namely, those of Janet, Freud, Adler, and Jung. Thirdly, the history is treated in a double perspective—what the various systems and episodes meant to contemporaries and what they mean to us; such a dual interpretation involves the author in writing several sections dealing with background material and milieu.

Professor Ellenberger's comprehensive history treats numerous thinkers, many of whom have extraordinary intellectual range. He is a polymath himself and equal to the imposing challenge. His 900 page volume, with well over 2500 footnotes, is the result of more than 12 years of research.

Neurodermatitis: A Case Presentation

S. Avissar-Suhami M.D.

S. Avissar-Suhami

S. Avissar-Suhami, M.D.
94 Rotchild Street
Petah-Tikva, Israel

S. Avissar-Suhami  

THREE YEARS AGO, DURING the spring, a 48 year old female was admitted to our hospital.1 She had been referred by the Department of Dermatology, Hadassah Hospital, Tel-Aviv, where she had received four months of medical treatment, without improvement.

Her dermatological diagnosis was neurodermatitis. A psychiatric consultant diagnosed the etiology of her illness as psychological, not organic and referred her to our institution for psychiatric treatment.

ON ADMISSION. The patient looked much older than her actual age. She was undernourished and neglected in outward appearance. Her clothes were covered with blood and pus. She spoke continuously and very aggressively, jumping from subject to subject and being unable to sit in one place. During the entire intake interview she scratched her legs which were covered with open, infected sores, caused by the incessant scratching by her long dirty fingernails. She was incapable of concentrating and shouted repeatedly, "My head is burning." From time to time she trembled as if she had rigours. She cried and knocked her head against the wall, shouting, "Cure me, cure me, " and "If you don't succeed in curing me, give me poison so that I can die." To emphasize her words, she opened her bag several times and took out various jars of medicine claiming that she had received all possible treatments, and that there was nothing left for her but death. She looked around her with an expression of disbelief in the possibility of ever being cured. Her mood was tinged with depression.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION.

ON 15 DECEMBER 1972, in a lovely Georgian terraced house in Church Row, the most beautiful street in Hampstead, the country playground of Eighteenth Century London, Adrian Stokes (1902–1972) died quietly and with great dignity, painting to the very last despite the impairment from brain metastases of a rectal carcinoma. His life was both a private and a public one of unflagging devotion to art and to psychoanalysis—and to building a bridge between the two that will stand for generations.

MARTIN GROTJAHN has a peculiar habit when taking weekend walks with me. He can be startled by almost anything. If it is small enough he picks it up and if it is beautiful enough he carries it home. It may be a perforated stone at the beach, an odd piece of wood, a dried beetle, a rattle shed by a snake, a part of an antler, a chicken bone, a lichen, or a feather from a red tailed hawk. At home he affixes his loot on the wall of his room where the montage has grown to the dimension of a triptych, which he calls the "Garden of Eden." It makes an astonishing, pleasing harmony, but it startles the unprepared visitor.

Now there is a strong resemblance between this "Garden of Eden" and my friend's new book. Like his montage, it is composed of symbols Martin Grotjahn collected on his walk through life and his work as a psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, but mostly as a therapist. Each piece on the wall and chapter in the book is a trophy of suffering, reminiscent of work, courageous persistence and an unending ability to be startled and to see familiar things with unfamiliar eyes. Each chapter is symbolic of mastery of reality, be it inner or outer, concerned with life or with death. The book reflects his affection for family and friends, teachers, colleagues, and students. It also reflects his partial identification with many people from Oedipus to Hieronymus Bosch and Sigmund Freud. In each of them he finds an important missing piece of himself, and thus it becomes a part of his friends who read about it.

DAVID RAPPAPORT ONCE REMARKED during a workshop at the White Institute, circa 1954, that "We shouldn't kill each other over our theories." It used to be commonplace that psychoanalytic writers would describe man in terms of the arc-reflex model, the topographic model or the economic. Today it is more usual for therapists to introduce a fourth model — one in which real interpersonal experience of the person is considered as well as the fantasy. Those of us who remember the days when ego-psychology came to the fore remember the violence we felt that had been done to the libido theory. Today certain distinguished ego psychologists call for an end to the theory of the drive. The fact is that the use of an old internally consistent theory, useful in its own right, as a foundation for introducing concepts which are not derived from it confuses, confounds and ultimately diminishes it. In this way, seeing "new" in terms of the "old" restricts our perceptions. A theory should bring together a mass of seemingly unrelated data into a comprehensible whole so that there is clarification and direction for setting up testable hypotheses. "Energy distribution" which some speak of is unclear to me in these "new conglomerate" theories.

"Libido" is used the same way. Libido and "aggression" are used as metaphors for "good" and "bad." The Concept of Freedom

Sabert Basescu Ph.D.

Sabert Basescu

Sabert Basescu, Ph.D.
516 Hommocks Road
Larchmont, N.Y. 10538

Sabert Basescu  

A MAJOR CONCERN IN THE practice of psychotherapy is the patient's responsibility for himself. To what extent is he accountable to himself for what he is and does? Answers to this question revolve around the issue of choice, or freedom. There is no sense in referring to accountability without examining the status of the options available. Such an examination usually falls under the rubric of the free will—determinism controversy.

The contemporary form of this controversy arises, on the deterministic side, out of the application of natural science—specifically scientific materialism—to the understanding of human behavior. The free will side has its roots in the universally felt experience of freedom of choice.

The subjective experience of freedom is not unitary but can be described in a number of different but related dimensions. Freedom "from, " contrasted with freedom "to, " is one such dimension. Restrictions, constraints, and obligations, imposed rather than chosen, exist as an obstacle to the experience of freedom. Similarly, responsibilities and emotional attachments, chosen but then regretted, result in the same thing. Relief from these felt burdens is then experienced as freedom. A whole subcultural group some years ago, the Beatniks, prized freedom from personal attachments as a desired prerequisite for the good life. In contrast, freedom "to" focuses on one's availability to commit oneself. Active participation in the events of living, involvement in meaningful relationships, forming one's values are all accompanied by the experience of freedom. In fact, without this kind of participatory commitment, the simple freedom from constraint leads to the experience of emptiness.

DR. WAHL'S PAPER IS A USEFUL highlighting of certain aspects of the psychoanalytic situation in the treatment of "the rich, the famous, and the influential." Although the paper is discursive and touches on many matters, I believe that the phenomenon that is central to it is that of the stereotyping of individuals who are members of particular groups. Webster II defines a stereotype as "anything repeated or reproduced without variation; anything conforming to a fixed or general pattern and undistinguished by individual marks, …" Hence, notions that tend to fix and define all Jews, blacks, men, women, psychoanalysts, the rich, etc., are examples of stereotypes to the extent that the group encompassed are "undistinguished by individual marks."

Sullivan (1953) described stereotyping as a regular and, more or less, necessary function for the developing individual and suggested its appearance in the juvenile period. He noted,

if only because of the speed with which the awesome varieties of people and behavior are impressed on the juvenile, it is hard indeed to avoid organizing—accessible to awareness—crude classifications of people, performance and so on, which really are irrational and which later become troublesome stereotypes.

Rafael Springmann  

IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (Springmann, 1971) I suggested a rational approach to the classification of noninterpretative psychotherapeutic interventions. I based this on Ezriel's concept of object relations. Since then, I have gradually become aware that Ezriel's contribution (1956), (1959), (1967) to the theory and practice of psychotherapeutic interventions in general has not really been granted the attention it deserves. It is therefore my purpose in this paper to try to give these theories some of their due, to sketch their development, starting with a brief reference to the problem of negative therapeutic reaction, illustrating, as I go along, with clinical material from the literature and of my own.

The problem of negative therapeutic reactions, namely the aggravation of symptoms and/or appearance of overt anxiety following essentially correct interpretations, was called attention to by Freud himself early in his work, and later repeatedly referred to by him. At first, Freud (1918) attributed the phenomenon to a childish form of rebellion on the part of the patient; later (1937a), partly to guilt feelings and the need for self-punishment, and partly to the operation of the destructiveness of the death instinct.

Other authors have taken up the problem and dealt with it—each according to his conception of psychoanalytic theory. Thus Fairbairn (1943) attributed negative therapeutic reactions to the extreme anxiety aroused by psychoanalytic efforts to release internalized bad objects from repression. Strachey (1934) had tackled the problem from a different angle. He argued that material was never repressed without good reason; that by its very nature it must have aroused anxiety and that repression occurred mainly for this anxiety to be allayed.

IT HAS BEEN NOTED THAT depressive reactions occur in volunteers in service organizations, such as Peace Corps and VISTA, at various points in their training and field placements. By depressive reactions, it is not meant that all volunteers who experienced varying degrees of depression necessarily suffered from clinical decompensation. Indeed, Thomson and English (1963) stress that "The relatively low rate of returns gives the Peace Corps one of the best records ever achieved by an overseas program." These authors, among the first to report on the psychologic distress experienced by almost all volunteers, made the following interesting observations: First, nearly all the volunteers experienced anxiety in the first few weeks of placement in the host country. Second, they experienced periods of depression at between three and five months after placement. Third, the greatest number of dropouts of volunteers occurred during these two periods. The authors relate the period of depression to the particular point in time at which the volunteers first realized that early expectations for rapid achievement of goals were unrealistic.

Another interesting study was reported by Napolitano (1967), based on interviews of Peace Corps volunteers who had completed their two years of service. Napolitano's inquiry involved "depression crises"1 as well as the apparently milder "Peace Corps Blues." His group clearly was not disillusioned by the outcome of achievement. THIS IS A FASCINATING topic and adds to the discourse on counter-transference, a special case of counter-transference, inherent in the analysis of the rich, etc. Apparently the editor presented this paper because of the myriad doors it knocks on, not the voices in the rooms behind them.

80

The point about analysts' name-dropping being similar to patients' dreaming of intimacy with the famous is well taken. Is there literature about this? In the halls of a training institute we learn, too easily, and so well, that analysts are subject to the same needs as their patients; among others, avarice, competitiveness, nepotism, power. Let the analysts look to that. What more can we say about the patient when this occurs in the analyst? What has the patient recapitulated with the analyst? I have in mind Tauber's idea that counter-transference data can be used, not as confessional, but as counter-communication, and not necessarily verbalized. Meltzer has written succinctly that self-analysis is the analyst's interminable tool. Dr. Wahl evidently follows the counter-transference-as-resistance school of thinking, something to be eliminated, and misses what can be part of that delicate finesse of the process, which generates the excitement of a genuine intimate relationship.

There's the whole issue of social amenities (Freud, it is said, helped the ladies on with their overcoats), which obviously is analyzable, and with those to whom the deferential aspects of a relationship are taken for granted, is of evident significance. Who opens the door? Who enters or leaves the room first? Does the entry and exit choreography vary? Does one shake hands, etc.? It's not that we take these for granted or that no one has ever thought about them, but that we rarely inquire about the patient's perceptual experience and its referents, or even our own. The social expectations based on various class identities are certainly germane. The context in which tenderness is permissible (read "comfortable"—and to whom), and the analyzability of the class nature of frustrations has never been touched in the literature. Social groups differ in their perception of pain; responses to frustration also must have expectable social components. Responses to the content of humor, of teasing, those also being socially determined, and acceptable methods of expressing tenderness or hostility are also subject to inquiry.

THE RIVAL FACTION IN OUR own tradition shows us how we look to outsiders. Adrian Stokes wrote The Game That Must be Lost in the Kleinian tradition. His North American readers will likely weary of the few Kleinian first-principles. Splitting, projective identification, good object, bad object, part object, whole object, persecutory anxiety, depressive anxiety, and envy. Is there anything else? How tiresome to see the rich expression of human life reduced to this monotonous, improverished alphabet. There, alas, the American analyst captures the feeling of literary men, of historians, of theologians as they look on the psychoanalytic tradition generally. Do we fancy Melanie Klein an ancient cosmologist reincarnate, unaccountably stranded in a convention of modern scientists? Are these paranoid and depressive positions the Yin and the Yang by which the universe is governed? Are these good objects and bad objects, whole objects and part objects, the earth, air, fire and water, of which everything is composed and by which everything is explained? But that is exactly how the unenlightened see the whole of psychoanalysis, with its libido cathecting this and that, its stock rehearsals of oral, anal, phallic and genital cycles, its castration complexes and penis envy, its predictable translations that numb the mind.

THE TOPIC OF IDENTITY has always been the source of challenging questioning. What is the exact nature of what we term identity? Is it a link? Is it a force meant to support the cohesion of the self? Is it a relationship among multiple relations? Is it a feeling? Is it the expression of a specific unconscious phantasy? Is it a self-image or one assigned by others? Is it a combination of both perspectives, or something else, something different? Does it exist from the beginning of life or does it develop gradually in the course of evolution? What role does the body play in connection with the feeling of identity? Are individuation, sameness, and identity interchangeable concepts? IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (Schimel, 1972), I discussed the role of the power theme in the obsessional patient. This paper focusses on the form and structure of the behaviors of obsessionals in the psychoanalytic situation and presents an optimal strategy for psychoanalytic intervention deriving chiefly from the views of Wilhelm Reich (1933) and Harry Stack Sullivan (1940).

In this presentation1 the term character structure is used in the same sense as personality type. Sullivan (1940) attributed many of the phenomena observed in the obsessional person to an underlying character structure which he termed the negativistic personality. This cannot be equated with negativism, although negativism does play a significant role in the thoughts and overt behavior patterns of obsessionals. The level of development achieved by the negativistic personality is evident throughout the spectrum of functioning by the individual, including the panoply of behaviors observed in the analyst's office. An obsessional patient's thoughtful response to the doctor's equally thoughtful and careful interpretation can take the form of, "I think you may have a point there, doctor." The therapist may feel defeated, and the patient never realizes that he has rejected the doctor's precious formulation since his "characteristic" mode of rejection has appeared in a socially acceptable form and, of course, he doesn't feel angry.

FROM A PHYLOGENETIC VIEWPOINT, thinking can be said to have historically emerged out of the necessity that man must understand and solve his problems; that is, from the necessity to interact with the elements around him: other men and nature. Once thinking has been acquired and instrumentalized, it acts upon external reality, thus initiating a dialectical process in which the organization of facts and the resolution of tasks are indispensable for survival. Afterward man develops a need to solve problems reaching a higher level. Furthermore, in the elaborating process which ushers in the appearance of the concept, that is, the specific content of human thought, there is a last step consisting in the return to, an action of thought (through human action) upon the same reality that bred it so as to transform it. New motivations leading to the further development of thought will result from this interpenetrating activity.

The most important characteristic of the thinking process is that it leads to the solution of tasks which are immediately related to the requirements of human survival. Its content is the generalized reflection of reality which may reach different levels of abstraction and generalization.

Thinking is mainly determined by a dynamic interrelation with an object, in which the object, acting upon the individual's conscience by means of those laws governing thought, initiates a series of cognitive operations leading to the disclosure of the relationship with the object. ADOLESCENCE IS A UNIVERSAL phenomenon of human development characterized by puberty changes which are pressed by inner psychological demands and the cultural adjustments required by the community. At times these demands are synchronous and collaborative but at other times divisive, antagonistic, and disruptive.

Even though there is a universal recognition of adolescence as a stage in the development process ushered in by the maturation of the sexual gonads, the consequences of such changes vary from culture to culture and person to person. Sexually there are only slight differences between the genders determined largely by the mores and styles of the particular time and place. Each gender is pressing and pushing for heterosexual intimacy of all kinds and while the female has an earlier chronological start, in essence the goals are precisely similar. While the essential task is to move into adulthood by integrating one's sexual interest with the opposite sex, one must also accept responsibility for one's own independent social role as an adult which is closely tied to the community prevailing gender prejudices and moral requirements. Thus while the pressure appears to be initiated through a physiological mechanism it inevitably is influenced and affected by the cultural definitions of adulthood. Thus the issue of identity in the sense of discovering who and what one is and how one stands in relation to one's self in the adult world, becomes of crucial concern. Concurrent to these needs are many other tasks the adolescent must confront.

The adolescent needs to be accepted by his compeers, while finding suitable goals and values for himself. He must decide on his vocational preferences and develop skills to fulfill them.

"LIFE! It's a game and I know all the rules. Whether I win or lose, I don't give a damn. Let's say I find life amusing." Listening to this patient I was struck by his dry, serious tone of voice, his stiff carriage, and the expression on his face, tight with anxiety, and showing no trace of the amusement that life supposedly brought him. Why such a denial of life's importance, and indeed of his own? There was something distinctly defiant about his statements but to whom were they directed, and why? His idea that life was a game which he knew how to play, even if he did not get much out of it, was a desperate attempt to give some meaning to his life. We were to discover subsequently that he felt it had none, that the necessary sign posts were missing, and that he often wished he could put an end to his miserable game. A CLEAR CONCEPTUALIZATION of the therapeutic process and of what in a relationship contributes to therapeutic outcome, remains somewhat elusive and certainly controversial in the psychoanalytic literature. Benjamin Wolstein  

THE EXPERIENCE OF psychic uniqueness, as suffered and undergone, never becomes fully rational in empirical and systematic analysis. It always also remains partly arational, partly irrational. Only after its emergence into awareness may it be delineated and shared in relatedness and communication with others.

Nor, of course, need it be interpreted as extending outward from libido instincts (biological model) nor inward from ego-interpersonal relations (sociological model). However it may be interpreted, it is at least what it is experienced as being, a psychic process taking place under psychological conditions within a psychoanalytic field of inquiry (psychological model).2

If a sense of uniqueness is first irrational, disjunctive, private (unconscious), and sharing it makes it rational, integrative, public (conscious), clearly this emergent awareness during psychoanalytic therapy provides the important base for developing the individual self and the social persona. Someone is now here, so to speak, in the patient, who can hope to confront his problems in living; for he has, in fact, already changed their psychology.

In this paper, I consider some questions about making the irrational rational in psychoanalytic therapy, with special reference to the place of psychic uniqueness in that shared experience.

THERE IS, presently, considerable debate among psychoanalysts about the amount of patient—therapist interaction permissible and, indeed, requisite to the successful outcome of the therapeutic endeavor. Although there has been a decided consensual shift in the direction of more active interaction, less "blank screen" participation, it has not been continuous, harmonious or without acrimony. The strictly structured, anonymous therapist, the various interpersonal perspectives, the encounter therapist, and finally the evangelistic laying-on-of-hands (and, sometimes, taking-off-of-pants) therapists constitute a bumpy continuum, each station of which accuses the next most active of apostasy and self-indulgence. As in all wars, right is always on our side in the pursuit of the Holy Grail of intimacy, that special dimension of relatedness which most defines the climate of psychoanalytic change.

Intimacy, in this sense, may be considered the ambiance of engagement or closeness between therapist and patient which characterizes the "positive therapeutic alliance"—that state of good intent and hard work without which no degree of virtuosity nor depth of experience of the therapist can prevail. The concept, intimacy, unfortunately, denotes a very ambiguous felt state, difficult to formulate and, even more confusing, undergoing a continuous shift in its meaning.

WITH APOLOGIES TO Stephen Potter (1968), and some appreciation for his levity, the following vignettes give some idea of what supervision can become for the candidate. Notice the difficulties

248

in the collaborative effort. Later, it will be necessary to explore, in a more heuristic way, those disjunctions preventing supervisory collaboration.

Under Supervisorship, the following moves and countermoves apply:

1. Supervisor: Make the candidate as anxious as possible by not saying a word.

Candidate: Ignore this, pretend Supervisor has a severe laryngitis and hand him a cough drop.

2. Supervisor: Interject that whatever the Candidate says is indicative of being a dumb-bell by snickering.

Candidate: Agree with this, and when the analysis goes sour, add, "I recall quoting you here. …"

3. Supervisor: Frequently point out the Candidate's character disorder.

Candidate: Hand the supervisor a nail-clipper as he chews his nails, saying, "The human bite is the most infectious. …"

4. Supervisor: When the analysis goes poorly, talk about the schizophrenia in the patient, and wonder about analyzability.

Candidate: Request psychologicals from an optimistic psychologist.

5. Supervisor: Surround yourself with old books, mostly in German, and quote from your outstanding teachers. Name-drop and emphasize this.

FENICHEL (1945) ONCE SAID THAT there are many ways to treat neuroses, but there should be only one theory which explains all their effects. While we all likely agree with him, we differ widely on how the theory should look.

What is preventing the development of a theory capable of unifying psychotherapies, ranging from psychoanalysis to group, family, and behavior therapy? In this space it is impossible for me to deal with the hundreds of possible reasons. Even one subcategory —the use of ambiguous language, ill-defined concepts, and pseudodichotomies—is too large. Therefore, I will address myself to only one item of this subcategory, the intrapsychic—interpersonal dichotomy, using it as a starting point for theoretical considerations which could possibly contribute to the unification of our field. In this, an interdisciplinary approach is necessary, and I will draw on recent developments, ranging from perceptual and social psychology, to systems theory and the philosophy of science. I also have drawn from unification attempts as diverse as those of H. G. Mead, Brunswick, Masserman, N. Cameron, Skinner, and others.

WHO ASPIRES TO KNOW a man should leave him to one side as early as possible. This proposition of Van Der Berg becomes crucial in the case of Schreber: Daniel Paul must be found precisely where he is not to be found. In Schatzman's work we soon discover that in Schreber's "lava of spiritual catastrophe" the eyes that we see are not his: the look we discover in them is that of his father.

It is the look of the Other, when it is loving or friendly, which indicates to us that we are someplace. If the look invalidates us, disqualifies us, our arm no longer knows what it does nor that it does it: our body will no longer have the right of movement. The space which bestows meaning on Daniel Paul's movements is rooted in the severe look of the father, in the permanent memory of his errors that the punishment board imposes on him. His movements and his nonmovements, his rigidity, are what they are thanks to the movements of those who surround him. The landscape-world thus acquires a meaning: the state of Schreber's murdered soul finds its context there and, consequently, its meaning.

IN THIS PAPER WE WILL discuss some concepts of psychosis, its clinical manifestations, and certain hypotheses as to its origin and evolution. Bion considers the concept of psychotic personality of fundamental importance to the understanding of phenomena associated with the psychotic process, regarding the psychotic personality as a mental state whose characteristics give rise to all those manifestations that are observable, in one form or another, in seriously disturbed patients.

The papers published by Bion on subjects related to psychosis come chronologically after his work on groups. Some of those papers are predominantly clinical and include case reports, while others are more theoretical and formulate hypotheses related, among other things, to language and thought in the schizophrenic. The papers written during this period (1950–1962) were later republished in his book Second Thoughts(1967), where they are rediscussed as a whole in the final commentary.

The patients, whose treatment has served as a basis for some of the hypotheses put forward in this chapter, were attended by Bion in a psychoanalytical setting no different from that normally used with neurotic patients, although in some cases the patients had a diagnosis of schizophrenia. The technique employed was always exclusively interpretive, both the positive and the negative transference being taken into account. In the interpretation of the material use was made of the Kleinian theories of part—object relationships, the paranoid—schizoid and depressive positions, the theory of envy, and the theory of early defence mechanisms, especially splitting and projective identification.

RECENTLY ON THREE SEPARATE occasions during conversation with colleagues I was astonished to hear from them inappropriate disclosures of patient identification or material. It was all the more surprising since I knew each of them to be excellent clinicians, experienced, conscientious men who took very seriously their Hippocratic responsibilities to patients. None of them seemed to be aware of the inappropriateness of their communication and, more significantly, in each instance the indiscreet communication related to a person of celebrity or influence.

This set me to thinking about the analysis of the rich, the famous, and the influential and to considering some of the special features that can often characterize the analysis of such patients and of the transference and the counter-transference that can be evoked therein. Since parenthetically it had always been a longstanding clinical impression of mine that many more patients in these three categories had had incomplete, ineffective, or unsatisfactory analytic experiences than is encountered in any other category of patient.

I remember some years ago being told by a patient of celebrity who had been unsuccessful in two previous therapeutic efforts, "Both of the doctors were more like friends than doctors. They fawned on me, seemed to want to know me as a friend and one of them even asked me for an autograph for his daughter.

Leon Hammer  

I

DURING 1971 I SPENT four months at the Community, which is a continuation of Kingsley Hall. I learned then, among other things about myself and others, that so-called "blow-out" centers, such as this one, correctly recognize the need people have to disorganize. I also came to recognize the incomplete truth in this idea, since it is incorrectly assumed by some that disorganization is an act of growth in itself. My belief is that disorganization leads to endless chaos unless other conditions for growth exist simultaneously. It is toward an exploration of these conditions within the framework of psychotherapies that this paper is directed. In this paper I will initiate a clinical discussion around three constants: experience, dependency, and contact.

Experience, roughly defined by Buber's "relationship, " is the irreducible absolute of human growth essential to human physical and psychological survival. Contact is the facilitator and journeyman of experience. Whereas experience is that which is undergone, contact is the living act, the concrete involvement, the labor and craft of experience. The primacy of contact and experience as constants of human growth renders man almost infinitely dependent on his own kind. These three primary constants are the matrix around which are woven all basic human needs.

The first opportunity for "new experience" in therapy is contact with the patient's so-called "resistance." Resistance is understood here to be the expression of the patient's defensive self-system in the therapeutic situation. The patient's defensive system is essentially a mode of relating designed to maintain life-giving contact with people without risking pain, hurt, or annihilation.

Lawrence Friedman M.D.

Lawrence Friedman

Lawrence Friedman, M.D.
50 East 72nd Street

Lawrence Friedman  

Edgar A. Levenson: The Fallacy of Understanding New York: Basic Books, 1972. 236 pages, $7.95

WE HAVE COME TO EXPECT a new conception of psychotherapy to be a great bore. We will be asked to accept another batch of neologisms (Vector Therapy; Being-in-the-World), and will watch an alleged innovation rudely elbow aside all previous understanding ("Anxiety is nothing but stage fright"). A thin ray of light comes shrouded in a thick fog of statistics about therapy variables and outcomes, or is refracted completely into a prescription for therapeutic behavior (confrontation, implosion, etc.).

By now it seems unlikely that we have completely overlooked a major, grossly different, useful way of talking with patients. What we need and rarely get is simply a new view of what we do as psychotherapists, how this squares with what we think we do, and how thinking about it differently might improve our effort.

Edgar Levenson's The Fallacy of Understanding is such a rare contribution. Brilliant and true, it is in its line the next significant book after Frank's Persuasion and Healing, but it is a much more important book because the anthropological facts that impressed Frank have been roughly common knowledge, while the highly abstract background of Levenson's thinking is not.

Yet this is not a book of precious esoterica. Neither a ponderous Germanic system, nor an elegant French terminologic love-affair, it has been appropriately packaged by the publisher as an honest, 19th century English philosophical essay, plain-spoken, personal, comprehensible, and always directly related to experience. There is wizardry in making so fundamental a book on psychotherapy brief and comprehensible.

CHANGES IN THE intimacy of social intercourse since World War II have brought about changes in the manifestations of transference and countertransference in psychoanalytic inquiry, and the resulting changes in the actual therapeutic conditions of the analysis of transference and countertransference have, in turn, brought about changes in the experience of intimacy between the psychoanalyst and his patient.

There are many important philosophical and cultural aspects of these various changes to be considered—problems of freedom, choice, and responsibility; automated technology and atomic energy; instant mass communication, space travel, and thermonuclear warfare; minority group unrest and mid-cult anonymity; generation gap and urban malaise; racial and sexual aspirations for equality; humanist versus materialist beliefs and values; respect, love, and compassion for our fellow man. However it is my objective in our panel, tonight, to treat their import from within the evolution and development of psychoanalysis itself.

THIS IS ONE OF A SERIES of papers1 on identification, individuation, the emergence of human relatedness, and the nature of the human bond (Schecter, 1968a), (1969), (1971) —all based on the premise that observations of normal psychic development can contribute to the deepening of psychoanalytic theory and therapy. Some observations relevant to this endeavor are derived from a formal seven-year research project on early ego development, more years of one-way screen teaching observations on "normal" development as well as from psychoanalytic practice—and just plain living experience.

From infancy through old age we are "possessed"—in various degrees of differentiation—by ideal images and concepts that have a certain peremptory quality in the organization of our experience. Hence, Freud (1914), (1923) resorted to the personifications Super -Ego and Ego-Ideal to metapsychologically cover many of the experiences we will be concerned with here on the phenomenological level. With each new stage or crisis of personality development the person may find an opportunity—and socially he is often given the adaptational task—of transforming the shape of the ideal self and other—and their relationships—in a direction that is at the same time more realistic, and yet hopefully not overlycynical and bitter in its disillusionment. As Winnicott has demonstrated, illusions are necessary for the growth of imagination.

WHEN DESCRIBING THE fundamental characteristics of schizophrenia Bleuler (1911), (1912) included what he called autism, which implies: detachment and withdrawal from reality; absolute or relative predominance of internal life; a loss of the sense of reality; and autistic (or dereistic) thinking.

Since Bleuler, two ways of thinking about autism have developed: On the one hand the concept of autism was limited to the idea of withdrawal and detachment, with the building of a "wall" which divided the person from the external world. This probably occurred in psychiatric thinking due to the widespread influence of Kanner's (1966) description of early infantile autism. On the other hand, and paradoxically, the concept was reduced to "a loss of the sense of reality." Autism proved to be, in this second interpretation, not simply a withdrawal but also an expansion, and, furthermore, an activity of which the fundamental characteristic was the predominance of internal life without withdrawal: dereistic thinking. Rapaport (1959), commenting upon Bleuler's paper of 1912, says that according to Bleuler, autism includes withdrawal as well as autistic thinking, and that the sole existence of autistic thinking is not autism.

According to Bleuler, realistic thinking and autism (or dereistic thinking) can exist together. He admits cases in which autism may be partial.

PARENT LOSS IS A SHORTHAND term describing a population of adult patients who have sustained, during childhood, the loss of a parent by death. This special group of patients has become increasingly visible within the last 20 years because of a combination of clinical observations and theoretical questions that needed answers. These questions have initiated an intensive study of this group of patients. In the beginning, attention was directed toward them because of an unexpected impasse in therapeutic efforts (Fleming, 1963). Attempts to explain this impasse led to insight in diagnostic understanding which led, in turn, to modifications of technique and to new correlations of old concepts. The new formulations in the areas of diagnosis and technique have been found useful in helping patients who come under the rubric "parent loss." These formulations have also contributed to the growing body of knowledge referable to developmental theory, e.g., self—object relationships, reality testing, and the phenomena of transference.

That is a very brief and generalized statement of the outcome in a long and on-going study of the questions raised by this group of patients. What I want to do in the next half hour is to discuss some of these questions as they come up in the diagnostic process and to present some clinical material that demonstrates the need to recognize the importance of certain developmental experiences in understanding the problems which bring an adult into therapy.

The problem of diagnosis in these cases is an interesting one in that it has implications for prevention as well as treatment.

Leo Katz Ph.D.

Leo Katz

Leo Katz, Ph.D.

Leo Katz  

MUCH ATTENTION HAS been paid to the effects on children of being rejected by their parents. Rejection has been described, not only in its overt forms, but also in its more subtle, indirect forms which often may look superficially like praise, support, loyalty, or admiration. The blind insistence by a parent, for example, that his child is a good child and can do no wrong often hides a rejecting attitude.

The phenomenon described in this paper is based on a rejecting attitude. It takes the form of overvaluation, i.e., an exaggeratedly high appraisal of the child's genuine capacity.

One of Grimm's fairy tales, Rumpelstiltskin, gives an account of such overvaluation and the trouble it can produce for the child. A brief synopsis follows.

A miller had an only daughter of whom he was very proud. One day he had to go to Court for an audience with the King during which the miller bragged about his daughter's accomplishments. He claimed that she could spin straw into gold. The King had the daughter brought to the Court, with the command to produce gold. To deliver, the daughter makes a pact with a dwarf who agrees to do the work in return for her promise to give up her first born child to him. In her desperation, the daughter agrees to these terms and all the straw the King provides is turned into gold. The King greatly admires her for her presumed skill and makes her his wife. After a year, a child is born. Soon thereafter, the dwarf appears to claim the child. The miller's daughter, now turned Queen, is unwilling to honor her contract. She pleads with the dwarf to show mercy and he gives her one chance to keep her child. If she can guess the dwarf's name, the contract is null and void. By means of stealth and the dwarf's own imprudence, the Queen discovers the dwarf's name, which is Rumpelstiltskin, and the dwarf is thwarted (Abbott, 1920).

The fairy tale describes in symbolic form the fate of an overvalued child. The trouble starts with an inaccurate evaluation of another person.
